lines.text: On November 18th, 1883, clocks across America did something strange.
At noon, New York's clocks were set back about four minutes, and noon struck a second time.
It's remembered as the day of two noons. And the reason was the railroads.
Until then, most towns kept their own time: noon was when the sun stood highest.
And because the Earth turns, noon slides west, four minutes for every degree of longitude.
Noon in Chicago was half past twelve in Pittsburgh.
For most people, that hardly mattered. But for railroads, it was chaos.
Each railroad kept its own time, and some stations hung a separate clock for every line.
So the railroads fixed it themselves: four zones, one hour apart, measured from Greenwich, England.
Inside a zone, every clock agreed. Cross a line, and the time jumped an hour.
A year later, 25 nations met in Washington and chose Greenwich as the prime meridian.
But Congress didn't write standard time into law until 1918, thirty-five years after the trains.
The hour on your phone didn't start with the sun, or with Congress. It started with a train schedule.
